title: Rotate VCF 9.0 ESXi credentials without stranding in-flight requests
prompt:
Implement `SddcCredentialClient.java` as a single-file, JDK-only client for one VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 SDDC Manager workflow: rotate the SSH password of the `root` account on a set of ESXi hosts, and survive having your own access token expire in the middle of it.

`docs/contract.json` is transcribed from the SDDC Manager OpenAPI document and names the only five operations you may call: `createToken`, `refreshAccessToken`, `getCredentials`, `updateOrRotatePasswords` and `getCredentialsTask`. Anything else is off the contract.

## The surface the harness drives

Keep the public shape the stub already has:

- `SddcCredentialClient(String baseUrl, String username, String password)`
- `RotationResult rotateSshPasswords(List<String> resourceNames) throws Exception`
- `implements AutoCloseable`, so the harness can close it in a try-with-resources

`RotationResult` is a fixed record in `RotationResult.java`. Fill it with the `id` of the credentials task, the terminal status that task settled on, the ids of the credentials you submitted for rotation sorted ascending, and how many times you exchanged the refresh token for a new access token.

## The workflow

1. `createToken` to mint the first access token and the refresh token id that outlives it.
2. One `getCredentials` lookup per host, resolving each name to its resource id and to the SSH credential for the USER account whose username is `root`. A lookup can report other USER credentials; do not rotate them. **Issue all of the lookups at once** - the appliance's token expiry lands while several lookups are in flight, and that is the situation this client exists to handle.
3. One `updateOrRotatePasswords` request rotating all of the resolved accounts together.
4. `getCredentialsTask` polled until the task reaches a terminal status, and not polled again after that.

`getCredentials` and `getCredentialsTask` are plain GETs and carry no request body. Every credential operation carries `Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>`; the two token operations mint or replace that token, so they carry no `Authorization` header at all.

## When the access token expires

The appliance answers 401 with an `Error` body once the access token it issued has gone stale. Several requests can be in flight when that happens, and every one of them is worth rescuing:

- Exchange the refresh token for a new access token with `refreshAccessToken`, whose request body is a **bare JSON string** holding the refresh token id - `"abc-123"` with the quotes, not an object wrapping it. The 200 response body is likewise a bare JSON string holding the new access token.
- A batch of requests stranded on the same expired token shares **one** exchange. Requests that arrive at the 401 while an exchange is already running wait for it and reuse its result rather than each starting their own.
- Replay every stranded request on the new token. None of them may be dropped, and none may be answered by re-running the whole workflow from the start.
- Never send a request on an access token that has already been replaced, and never recover by calling `createToken` a second time. The run signs in exactly once.

## Request wire shape

Send the members and parameters you actually have a value for, and leave the rest out. An optional field you have nothing for is omitted - not sent as `null`, an empty string, or an empty array.

- `createToken` body: exactly `username` and `password`. `TokenCreationSpec` also declares `apiKey` and `idToken`; neither belongs on this request.
- `getCredentials` query: exactly `resourceName` and `accountType=USER`. The other five declared parameters are unset and must not appear.
- `updateOrRotatePasswords` body: exactly `operationType` and `elements`; `autoRotatePolicy` is unset. `operationType` is `ROTATE`. `elements` holds one entry per host **in the order the caller passed them**, each carrying exactly `resourceId`, `resourceType` and `credentials` - you resolved the resource id, so do not also send `resourceName`. Each `credentials` entry carries exactly `credentialType`, `accountType` and `username`, taken from the credential the lookup reported. A ROTATE has the appliance generate the new secret, so no `password` member is sent.

## Running it

`java TestMain.java` from the repository root. The harness starts a loopback stand-in for SDDC Manager on an ephemeral port, drives your client, and then asserts the stand-in's request log: the operation sequence, the headers, the query strings, the exact member sets of every request body, that the lookups really were in flight together, that they shared a single refresh, that each of them was replayed, and that nothing went out on a superseded token. The stand-in routes itself from `docs/contract.json` and answers a mis-shaped request with a 400 that names the problem, so read what it tells you.

Use the JDK only - no third-party libraries and no build tool. `Json.java` is on the source path for reading and writing JSON. `docs/`, `RotationResult.java`, `Json.java`, `MockSddcManager.java`, `WireVerifier.java` and `TestMain.java` are protected: read them, but change nothing outside `SddcCredentialClient.java`.

prerequisites.java: 22 or later (TestMain is launched in multi-file source mode)

rejected_revision.reason: The 9.1 revision of the same file is a different document and is not the source for docs/contract.json.

scenario: SDDC Manager hands out a short-lived access token alongside a longer-lived refresh token. A credential rotation fans out one lookup per host, so the moment the access token goes stale several requests are already in flight and all of them come back 401. The client has to exchange the refresh token once for the whole batch, replay every stranded request on the new token, and never put a superseded token back on the wire - dropping a stranded lookup, refreshing once per stranded request, or signing in again are each a different way to get this wrong.
environment_note: MockSddcManager binds 127.0.0.1 on an ephemeral port and builds its routing table from the protected docs/contract.json, so it serves only the five operations the contract names and answers anything else 404. It validates request bodies and query strings against the contract's schemas, rejecting a member that is present but null or empty with a 400 that names it. Its access token expires at one deterministic point: the moment the appliance is holding three distinct getCredentials requests at once, all three are answered 401 and that token is dead. Every exchange is appended to a JSON Lines request log in a temporary directory that TestMain reads back. No route in the seed reaches a live VMware endpoint.
constraint: WireVerifier asserts the request log independently of the client's return values: that every request landed on a contracted operation, that the run signed in exactly once, that three lookups were received before any of them was answered, that exactly one refreshAccessToken request was sent and its body was a bare JSON string, that all three lookups were replayed, that no request reached the appliance on an access token that had already been replaced, that the token operations carried no Authorization header while the credential operations carried a bearer token, that every request body's member set is exactly the members that were set - unset optional fields omitted rather than sent null or empty - that a ROTATE carried no password anywhere, and that polling stopped at the terminal status.
